title: Two Ways to Add Up
statement: How many positive integers less than $500$ can be written as a sum of $4$ consecutive positive integers and can also be written as a sum of $7$ consecutive positive integers? The two lists of consecutive integers need not be related to each other.
hints: Call the first number in each list $a$ or $b$, and write each sum as a simple expression in that letter. Also note the smallest value each sum can take.

Use remainders. The sum of four consecutive integers starting at $a$ is $4a + 6$, which always leaves remainder $2$ on division by $4$. The sum of seven consecutive integers starting at $b$ is $7b + 21$, which is always a multiple of $7$.

Test the multiples of $7$ by their remainders on division by $4$: the numbers that are multiples of $7$ and leave remainder $2$ on division by $4$ are exactly those of the form $14 + 28k$. A sum of seven consecutive positive integers is at least $1 + 2 + \dots + 7 = 28$, so $14$ is too small. Now count the allowed values below $500$.
solution:
A sum of 4 consecutive integers starting at $a$ is $4a+6$, so $N\equiv 2\pmod 4$ with $N\ge 10$. A sum of 7 consecutive integers starting at $b$ is $7(b+3)$, so $N$ is a multiple of $7$ with $N\ge 28$.

Conversely, take $N=7m$ with $m\ge 4$ and $N\equiv 2\pmod 4$. Since $7\equiv -1\pmod 4$, this means $m\equiv 2\pmod 4$, so $m=4k+2$ with $k\ge 1$ and $N=28k+14$. Then $a=7k+2$ and $b=4k-1$ are positive integers with $4a+6=7b+21=N$.

Now $28k+14<500$ gives $k\le 17$, since $28\cdot 17=476<486<504=28\cdot 18$. So $k=1,\dots,17$, giving $17$ numbers.
